title: Training the Next Generation of Reformers
author: Gregory Soderberg
summary: In his annual Reformation Day repost, Gregory Soderberg retells how Martin Luther posted the 95 Theses in 1517 as an academic discussion, not an act of rebellion, and why the timing around All Saints' Day mattered. He traces the Reformation to the Renaissance return to ancient sources, the printing press, and the scholarship of Erasmus and his associates such as Oecolampadius, who produced the first printed Greek New Testament. The key causal claim is that rediscovered Greek and Hebrew drove the Reformers' conclusions, and that they saw themselves as recovering what the church had universally held. From this he draws the mission of the contemporary classical Christian school movement: training students in the classics and ancient languages so they can bravely challenge the status quo. He closes by noting that most graduates will serve in ordinary vocations, and that the movement stands on the shoulders of giants.
points: Luther began as a doctor of theology raising an academic objection to indulgence preachers and had no intention of breaking with Rome.
The Reformation grew out of the Renaissance return to classical sources, amplified by the printing press and Erasmus's scholarship.
Study of biblical Greek and Hebrew was a main cause of the Reformation, and Oecolampadius is an example of a humanist scholar who became a Reformer.
The Reformers regarded themselves as truly catholic, seeking to restore what Christians had universally believed and practised.
Classical Christian schools aim to train ordinary faithful workers through the classics and languages, with some prepared to lead renewal.
quotes: Martin Luther did not mean to start the Reformation. In 1517, Luther, a teacher of theology in Germany, posted some items for an academic discussion on the church door in Wittenberg (really a community bulletin board back then).

At this point in his career, Luther had no intention to break away from the Roman Catholic church—as a “doctor” of theology Luther had the right, and the obligation, to express concerns about the church.

One of the main causes of the Reformation was the rediscovery of Biblical Greek and Hebrew. Most of the Reformers were serious students of Greek and Hebrew, and the insights they gained from this engagement with the Scriptures fueled the momentous changes that many of us celebrate around Oct. 31.

In northern Europe, the Renaissance took a more “bookish” turn. Sparked by Johannes Gutenberg’s invention of the movable-type printing press, northern Europeans could suddenly produce and exchange ideas quickly through the printed word.

Church historian Jaroslav Pelikan has called Martin Luther an “obedient rebel.” Luther did not intend to reject all of the Church’s teachings. Nor did he want to dismiss all of church history prior to the Reformation.
Catholicus means “universal,” and the early Reformers tried to reform Christian worship and church practices according to what Christians had “universally” believed and practiced.
Our students will most likely not be mentioned in later history books. Most will faithfully labor for the glory of God and the good of their communities, wherever God calls them to serve.
context: Luther's original act was an academic invitation, not a revolt.
Luther initially sought reform within the Roman church.
Recovery of biblical languages was a principal cause of the Reformation.
The printing press let Renaissance scholarship spread quickly in northern Europe.
The Reformers valued church history and did not reject all earlier tradition.
The Reformers framed their project as restoring universal Christian practice.
Classical Christian schools expect most graduates to serve in ordinary vocations.
